tweets.text: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

World Modeling with JEPA has recently gained traction thanks to a novel anti-collapse mechanism called "SIGReg" (by @ylecun and @randall_balestr ). The math is clean, but it is rarely explained from first principles, so I broke it down in a detailed blog post 📰 Here is the summary (🧵): The problem: in JEPA, both sides of the prediction loss go through the same encoder. Map every input to a single constant point, the predictor matches it trivially, and the loss hits exactly zero. Perfect score, zero information. Gradient descent finds this solution by default. Prior work patched around it with stop-gradients, EMA teacher-student models, frozen pretrained encoders, and VICReg-style losses with 6+ hand-tuned coefficients. Each adds instability, hyperparameters, or a dependency on someone else's pretraining. --- SIGReg replaces all of that with one regularizer built on a single claim: force the batch of embeddings to look like samples from an isotropic Gaussian, N(0, I). LeJEPA proves this isn't arbitrary. It's the distribution that minimizes worst-case downstream risk across linear and nonlinear probes. But "make the embeddings Gaussian" is easy to say and hard to compute. You can't estimate a density in 200+ dimensions from a small batch. The fix is a chain of four classical results: compare Fourier transforms instead of densities, turn that comparison into a single scalar, approximate the integral with ~16 points, and lift the whole thing from 1D to any dimension with a theorem from 1936. Each step is simple. The stack is what makes it work. Read the subsequent posts in this thread to understand each step. --- But why it provably works: the only distribution for which SIGReg = 0 is N(0, I), which is full rank by construction, with every eigenvalue equal to 1. A collapsed low-rank encoder cannot be a minimum. It's not just unlikely to converge there—it's mathematically excluded. And the training loop stays boring: total loss = prediction + λ·SIGReg The encoder gets gradients from both terms; the predictor gets gradients from the prediction term only. No alternating updates, no stop-gradients, no two-timescale tricks. Now check out the breakdown below. 👇

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). [Original text: The Batch]

Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access, other nations will rationally try to secure alternatives. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

Let us review task types and how to get data for them: Verifiable domains: For post training particularly, there are already vast amount of problem statements and solutions in millions of text books. Also, synthetically generating data (e.g. introducing bugs in programs) is an effective strategy. This works for verifiable domains like Code. Knowledge work domains: As for tasks like GDPEval etc. (e.g. spreadsheet making, making presentations etc.) you do need experts curating problem statements and ideal solutions; but it is not a rocket science. The reason you don't hear a lot about Chinese data labelling companies is the same why you don't hear a lot about Chinese IT service companies: they have limited themselves to the mainland where they have ample business. The open release of Kimi K3 once again shows that our interventions for resilience should be focused on a world where advanced AI is *abundant* rather than scarce. Sayash Kapoor (@sayashk) Many people have written about advanced AI being too restricted, but my fear is we haven’t planned enough for a world where advanced AI will continue to proliferate. This is despite the availability of models like GLM-5.2, despite the "Deepseek moment", and despite consistent evidence that open models lag closed models by a matter of months. What happens in a world where, even with restrictions on US frontier models and compute, advanced AI continues to be broadly available? Non-proliferation is likely to fail; at best, it provides a few months of buffer A common response is to dispute the premise by claiming that the narrow open vs. closed gap is only a result of distillation by Chinese model developers, and if the US ecosystem shut itself off, Chinese competitors won't be able to keep up. Maybe. But the evidence we have so far points the other way: 1) Existing defenses against distillation don't work. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google already censor their models' reasoning chains to prevent distillation, and Anthropic has prevented Chinese customers from accessing their models. This hasn't led to an increasing gap between closed and open models. 2) Chinese companies have made genuine improvements to their model training stack that are discounted too heavily by US observers. Notably, preventing distillation might systematically push Chinese AI labs to innovate, rather than follow the lead of US labs. 3) AI has also seen the equivalent of the "four-minute mile": once a developer shows what's possible, others can prioritize and quickly improve their models on those capabilities, even when they previously weren't able to. We've seen this with reasoning models (Deepseek R1), coding agents (GLM-5.2), and will likely continue to see it with future advances. 4) There are many improvements that don't require large training runs. Updating scaffolds, finetuning models, using more inference compute can all narrow the gap between the capabilities elicited from US and Chinese models, even if the gap between the base models increases. In other words, even if we ban open models, improving the agent scaffolds could lead to continued improvements in capabilities, such as by the creation of specialized scaffolds for cyberattacks (this is known as the "scaffold overhang"). So we are likely to continue seeing new misuse risks emerge for years. 5) Most importantly, there is no secret sauce for training advanced AI models. The main training techniques for developing and serving frontier models are well understood. Labs' roadmaps can be gleaned based on the roles they (and their third-party providers) are hiring for. The data being collected through these efforts doesn't require new innovations either. If non-proliferation can at most buy us a few months, we should use that time to improve resilience AI policy can't take for granted that US restrictions on models and compute will lead to a worldwide slowdown in the availability of advanced AI. What changes if we plan for a world with widespread access to advanced AI? For one, we need to prioritize resilience. If licensing, export controls, and other restrictions can at most give the government a few months of lead time, that time is best spent giving defenders broad and deep access to AI systems to improve our ability to withstand attacks. This becomes especially important since many of the misuse risks that the US govt. is concerned about, such as cyberattacks, are a result of AI's *absolute* capabilities, rather than *relative* the gap between open and closed models. For example, even if US model developers can maintain a lead compared to foreign developers, this doesn't help unless the lead is used to find and fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the meantime, as @joshua_saxe and others have argued. To their credit, OpenAI and Anthropic have both emphasized the importance of improving resilience. There is also widespread consensus within AI policy that resilience is important. But resilience is often still described as a way to improve society's ability to withstand the availability of *US* frontier models, controlled in its pace of diffusion by US companies and the government. This is also reflected in Anthropic's recent letter to US Senators, where they argue that if only we address distillation attacks and enforce export controls better, advanced AI capabilities would not be available broadly. Because of all the reasons mentioned above, I think this is unlikely. This makes investing in resilience that much more important. — https://nitter.net/sayashk/status/2071212404097048579#m

@MIT_CSAIL 's @a1zhang and @lateinteraction trained a model to generalize 8-32x past its training length. The research credits the harness, the scaffolding around the model, not the model itself. Train it only on short tasks, and it still handles far longer ones. That works because the harness keeps every model call close to what it was trained on. It offloads the bulk context into a code environment and keeps the results of its smaller sub-tasks out of the main chat, so the model never drowns in its own history. A few things that held up: > trains short, runs 8-32x longer > transfers across different domains > training costs 1.5-3x more Context rot, the decay your agent hits as history piles up, is often this scaffolding problem, not a weak model. So, > How do you tell rot from a model that is simply too weak? > When does adding a harness backfire? > What is the one check to run before you pay for a bigger model? Les outils évoluent rapidement, avec des fonctionnalités vocales, des applications dans la santé et la cyberdéfense. glossaire.definition: Un modèle d'IA capable de comprendre et de générer des informations à partir de différents types de données (texte, image, son, etc.).

Logiciel dont le code source est publiquement accessible, permettant à quiconque de le voir, le modifier et le distribuer.
L'art de formuler des instructions (prompts) pour obtenir les meilleurs résultats possibles d'un modèle d'IA.
L'unité de base que les modèles de langage utilisent pour traiter le texte ; un mot ou une partie de mot.

category_summaries.actu: Les grandes entreprises comme OpenAI, Google et Anthropic continuent de dévoiler leurs dernières innovations, notamment des modèles plus performants (Gemini 3.6 Flash, Claude 5.6), des fonctionnalités vocales intégrées et des applications dans des domaines comme la santé. highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'appuyer en arrière, passer en mode vocal et juste "divaguer" pendant environ 10 minutes, le chaos total, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview de quelques échanges. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus clairement que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit-machine et avez moins à corriger par la suite.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Lorsqu'un modèle génère du texte, une grande partie du temps est consacrée au déplacement de ses poids de la mémoire vers les unités de calcul. Le matériel optimisé pour l'inférence minimise ce mouvement, rendant la génération de jetons plusieurs fois plus rapide qu'avec une configuration GPU typique. Dans ce cours, le matériel que vous utiliserez est le Wafer-Scale Engine de Cerebras, conçu pour une inférence rapide en gardant les poids du modèle proches des unités de calcul. L'inférence rapide accélère les flux de travail longs et pilotés par des agents, et débloque également les applications sensibles à la latence et en temps réel comme la traduction en direct et les agents vocaux. highlights.text_original: New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively. Avec l'âge, le sucre se lie aux protéines, créant des cicatrices chimiques rigides et collantes qui affectent la peau, les artères, les yeux et plus encore. On pensait que c'était irréversible et maintenant cela pourrait être réversible, restaurant un état sain. Les chercheurs l'ont fait en utilisant AlphaFold pour rechercher 45 000 oxydases, puis ont criblé plus de 500 millions de variants modifiés par évolution dirigée. Le travail est encore ex vivo dans un laboratoire. Livrer une enzyme bactérienne volumineuse en toute sécurité dans des tissus vivants, avec une pénétration et une biodisponibilité suffisantes, reste un défi majeur. — https://nitter.net/bryan_johnson/status/2077789855434879292#m

actu.text_fr: La sortie ouverte de Kimi K3 montre une fois de plus que nos interventions pour la résilience devraient se concentrer sur un monde où l'IA avancée est *abondante* plutôt que rare. Sayash Kapoor (@sayashk) Beaucoup de gens ont écrit sur le fait que l'IA avancée est trop restreinte, mais ma peur est que nous n'ayons pas assez planifié pour un monde où l'IA avancée continuera de proliférer. Et ce, malgré la disponibilité de modèles comme GLM-5.2, malgré le "moment Deepseek", et malgré des preuves constantes que les modèles ouverts ont quelques mois de retard sur les modèles fermés. Que se passe-t-il dans un monde où, même avec des restrictions sur les modèles de pointe américains et le calcul, l'IA avancée reste largement disponible ? La non-prolifération va probablement échouer ; au mieux, elle fournit quelques mois de délai. Une réponse courante consiste à contester la prémisse en affirmant que l'écart étroit entre ouvert et fermé n'est que le résultat de la distillation par les développeurs de modèles chinois, et que si l'écosystème américain se coupait du reste, les concurrents chinois ne pourraient pas suivre. Peut-être. Mais les preuves dont nous disposons jusqu'à présent vont dans l'autre sens : 1) Les défenses existantes contre la distillation ne fonctionnent pas. OpenAI, Anthropic et Google censurent déjà les chaînes de raisonnement de leurs modèles pour empêcher la distillation, et Anthropic a empêché les clients chinois d'accéder à leurs modèles. Cela n'a pas conduit à un écart croissant entre les modèles fermés et ouverts. 2) Les entreprises chinoises ont apporté des améliorations réelles à leur pile d'entraînement de modèles qui sont trop sous-estimées par les observateurs américains. Notamment, empêcher la distillation pourrait pousser systématiquement les laboratoires d'IA chinois à innover, plutôt que de suivre l'exemple des laboratoires américains. 3) L'IA a également vu l'équivalent du "mile en quatre minutes" : une fois qu'un développeur montre ce qui est possible, d'autres peuvent prioriser et améliorer rapidement leurs modèles sur ces capacités, même lorsqu'ils n'en étaient pas capables auparavant. Nous avons vu cela avec les modèles de raisonnement (Deepseek R1), les agents de codage (GLM-5.2), et nous continuerons probablement à le voir avec les progrès futurs. 4) Il existe de nombreuses améliorations qui ne nécessitent pas de longues sessions d'entraînement. La mise à jour des échafaudages, le réglage fin des modèles, l'utilisation de plus de calculs d'inférence peuvent tous réduire l'écart entre les capacités obtenues à partir des modèles américains et chinois, même si l'écart entre les modèles de base augmente. En d'autres termes, même si nous interdisons les modèles ouverts, l'amélioration des échafaudages d'agents pourrait entraîner des améliorations continues des capacités, par exemple par la création d'échafaudages spécialisés pour les cyberattaques (c'est ce qu'on appelle le "dépassement d'échafaudage"). Nous sommes donc susceptibles de continuer à voir émerger de nouveaux risques d'utilisation abusive pendant des années. 5) Le plus important est qu'il n'y a pas de recette secrète pour entraîner des modèles d'IA avancés. Les principales techniques d'entraînement pour développer et déployer des modèles de pointe sont bien comprises. Les feuilles de route des laboratoires peuvent être déduites des rôles pour lesquels ils (et leurs fournisseurs tiers) embauchent. Les données collectées par ces efforts ne nécessitent pas non plus de nouvelles innovations. Si la non-prolifération ne peut au mieux nous acheter que quelques mois, nous devrions utiliser ce temps pour améliorer la résilience. La politique d'IA ne peut pas présumer que les restrictions américaines sur les modèles et le calcul entraîneront un ralentissement mondial de la disponibilité de l'IA avancée. Qu'est-ce qui change si nous planifions pour un monde avec un accès généralisé à l'IA avancée ? D'une part, nous devons donner la priorité à la résilience. Si les licences, les contrôles à l'exportation et d'autres restrictions ne peuvent donner au gouvernement qu'un délai de quelques mois, il est préférable de consacrer ce temps à donner aux défenseurs un accès large et approfondi aux systèmes d'IA pour améliorer notre capacité à résister aux attaques. Cela devient particulièrement important étant donné que de nombreux risques d'utilisation abusive qui préoccupent le gouvernement américain, tels que les cyberattaques, résultent des capacités *absolues* de l'IA, plutôt que de l'écart *relatif* entre les modèles ouverts et fermés. Par exemple, même si les développeurs de modèles américains peuvent maintenir une avance par rapport aux développeurs étrangers, cela n'aide pas à moins que l'avance ne soit utilisée pour trouver et corriger les vulnérabilités de cybersécurité entre-temps, comme l'ont soutenu @joshua_saxe et d'autres. À leur crédit, OpenAI et Anthropic ont tous deux souligné l'importance d'améliorer la résilience. Il existe également un consensus général dans la politique d'IA sur l'importance de la résilience. Mais la résilience est souvent encore décrite comme un moyen d'améliorer la capacité de la société à résister à la disponibilité des modèles de pointe *américains*, dont le rythme de diffusion est contrôlé par les entreprises américaines et le gouvernement. Ceci est également reflété dans la récente lettre d'Anthropic aux sénateurs américains, où ils soutiennent que si nous abordons les attaques de distillation et appliquons mieux les contrôles à l'exportation, les capacités avancées d'IA ne seront pas largement disponibles. Pour toutes les raisons mentionnées ci-dessus, je pense que cela est peu probable. Cela rend l'investissement dans la résilience d'autant plus important. — https://nitter.net/sayashk/status/2071212404097048579#m
actu.text_original: The open release of Kimi K3 once again shows that our interventions for resilience should be focused on a world where advanced AI is *abundant* rather than scarce. Sayash Kapoor (@sayashk) Many people have written about advanced AI being too restricted, but my fear is we haven’t planned enough for a world where advanced AI will continue to proliferate. This is despite the availability of models like GLM-5.2, despite the "Deepseek moment", and despite consistent evidence that open models lag closed models by a matter of months. What happens in a world where, even with restrictions on US frontier models and compute, advanced AI continues to be broadly available? Non-proliferation is likely to fail; at best, it provides a few months of buffer A common response is to dispute the premise by claiming that the narrow open vs. closed gap is only a result of distillation by Chinese model developers, and if the US ecosystem shut itself off, Chinese competitors won't be able to keep up. Maybe. But the evidence we have so far points the other way: 1) Existing defenses against distillation don't work. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google already censor their models' reasoning chains to prevent distillation, and Anthropic has prevented Chinese customers from accessing their models. This hasn't led to an increasing gap between closed and open models. 2) Chinese companies have made genuine improvements to their model training stack that are discounted too heavily by US observers. Notably, preventing distillation might systematically push Chinese AI labs to innovate, rather than follow the lead of US labs. 3) AI has also seen the equivalent of the "four-minute mile": once a developer shows what's possible, others can prioritize and quickly improve their models on those capabilities, even when they previously weren't able to. We've seen this with reasoning models (Deepseek R1), coding agents (GLM-5.2), and will likely continue to see it with future advances. 4) There are many improvements that don't require large training runs. Updating scaffolds, finetuning models, using more inference compute can all narrow the gap between the capabilities elicited from US and Chinese models, even if the gap between the base models increases. In other words, even if we ban open models, improving the agent scaffolds could lead to continued improvements in capabilities, such as by the creation of specialized scaffolds for cyberattacks (this is known as the "scaffold overhang"). So we are likely to continue seeing new misuse risks emerge for years. 5) Most importantly, there is no secret sauce for training advanced AI models. The main training techniques for developing and serving frontier models are well understood. Labs' roadmaps can be gleaned based on the roles they (and their third-party providers) are hiring for. The data being collected through these efforts doesn't require new innovations either. If non-proliferation can at most buy us a few months, we should use that time to improve resilience. AI policy can't take for granted that US restrictions on models and compute will lead to a worldwide slowdown in the availability of advanced AI. What changes if we plan for a world with widespread access to advanced AI? For one, we need to prioritize resilience. If licensing, export controls, and other restrictions can at most give the government a few months of lead time, that time is best spent giving defenders broad and deep access to AI systems to improve our ability to withstand attacks. This becomes especially important since many of the misuse risks that the US govt. is concerned about, such as cyberattacks, are a result of AI's *absolute* capabilities, rather than *relative* the gap between open and closed models. For example, even if US model developers can maintain a lead compared to foreign developers, this doesn't help unless the lead is used to find and fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the meantime, as @joshua_saxe and others have argued. To their credit, OpenAI and Anthropic have both emphasized the importance of improving resilience. There is also widespread consensus within AI policy that resilience is important. But resilience is often still described as a way to improve society's ability to withstand the availability of *US* frontier models, controlled in its pace of diffusion by US companies and the government. This is also reflected in Anthropic's recent letter to US Senators, where they argue that if only we address distillation attacks and enforce export controls better, advanced AI capabilities would not be available broadly. Because of all the reasons mentioned above, I think this is unlikely. This makes investing in resilience d'autant more important. — https://nitter.net/sayashk/status/2071212404097048579#m
actu.decryptage: Distillation d'IA : technique où un modèle plus petit apprend à imiter le comportement d'un modèle plus grand et plus performant. Non-prolifération : l'idée de limiter la diffusion de technologies avancées pour des raisons de sécurité.

actu.text_fr: je ne crois pas que la réalité soit une simulation, mais on ne pourrait vraiment pas écrire ce scénario : • Il y a deux semaines : À l'AI Engineer World's Fair de @swyx à SF, j'ai décidé à la dernière minute d'introduire mon ami @uri_rolls sur scène pour sa conférence sur les benchmarks cybernétiques pour la pénétration d'infrastructure et le contrôle d'accès (voir ci-dessous, équipe incroyable). J'ai dit : "Il y a un avenir où la cyberdéfense est vivante et tout le monde est bien protégé et je suis presque sûr que cet avenir implique des modèles open-source." Et plus tard : "Un grand défi sera la vitesse : la vitesse de l'attaque par rapport à la défense. Quand un intrus commence à entrer, vous devez voir ce qui se passe et l'attraper." • Il y a une semaine : @huggingface est touché par une intrusion sophistiquée pendant le week-end. Les traces ressemblent à tout ce que nous avons vu auparavant et suggèrent une implication sérieuse de l'IA, mais nous ne savons pas encore quel modèle a été utilisé. Les modèles fermés que nous demandons pour nous aider s'étouffent dans leurs garde-fous. Nous devons réagir vite, alors nous nous tournons vers le GLM-5.2 de @Zai_org pour nous aider à analyser l'attaque. • Plus tôt cette semaine : @OpenAI nous contacte, révèle ce qui s'est passé et s'associe à nous pour l'enquête. L'intrus s'avère être exactement ce que nous avions discuté il y a deux semaines : un agent entièrement autonome, alimenté par un modèle de pointe non publié, tentant d'accéder à une partie de notre infrastructure. Parfois, la chronologie dans laquelle nous vivons donne le vertige.
actu.text_original: I don’t believe reality is a simulation, but you genuinely couldn’t script this timeline: • Two weeks ago: At @swyx ’s AI Engineer World’s Fair in SF, I decide at the last minute to introduce my friend @uri_rolls onstage for his talk on cyber benchmarks for infrastructure penetration and access control (see below, amazing team). I say: “There is a future where cyber is alive and everyone is well protected and I’m pretty sure that future involves open-source models.” And later: “A big challenge is going to be speed: the speed of attack versus defense. When an intruder starts to enter, you have to see what’s happening and catch them.” • One week ago: @huggingface is hit by a sophisticated intrusion over the weekend. The traces look unlike anything we’ve seen before and suggest serious AI involvement, but we don’t yet know which model was used. The closed models we ask for help choke on their guardrails. We need to react fast, so we turn to @Zai_org ’s GLM-5.2 to help us analyze the attack. • Earlier this week: @OpenAI reaches out, discloses what happened, and partners with us on the investigation. The intruder turns out to be exactly what we had discussed two weeks earlier: a fully autonomous agent, powered by an unreleased frontier model, attempting to gain access to part of our infrastructure. Sometimes the timeline we live in is genuinely vertigo-inducing. Video

On pensait que c'était irréversible et maintenant cela pourrait être réversible, restaurant un état sain. Les chercheurs l'ont fait en utilisant AlphaFold pour rechercher 45 000 oxydases, puis ont criblé plus de 500 millions de variants modifiés par évolution dirigée. Le travail est encore ex vivo dans un laboratoire. Livrer une enzyme bactérienne volumineuse en toute sécurité dans des tissus vivants, avec une pénétration et une biodisponibilité suffisantes, reste un défi majeur. — https://nitter.net/bryan_johnson/status/2077789855434879292#m

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'appuyer en arrière, passer en mode vocal et juste "divaguer" pendant environ 10 minutes, le chaos total, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview de quelques échanges. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus clairement que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit-machine et avez moins à corriger par la suite.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. tips.text_fr: La "boucle d'ingénierie" est un buzzword populaire après que les mentions par Boris Cherny (créateur de Claude Code) et Peter Steinberger (créateur d'OpenClaw) soient devenues virales sur les réseaux sociaux. Les boucles sont maintenant une partie essentielle de la façon dont nous amenons les agents IA à itérer en longueur pour construire des logiciels. Dans cette lettre, je voudrais partager mes 3 boucles clés, montrées dans l'image ci-dessous, pour construire des produits de 0 à 1. Ces boucles guident non seulement la façon dont je construis des logiciels, mais aussi la façon dont je décide quels logiciels construire. Boucle de codage d'agent : Étant donné une spécification de produit et éventuellement un ensemble d'évaluations (c'est-à-dire un ensemble de données contre lequel mesurer la performance), nous pouvons demander à un agent IA d'écrire du code, de tester son travail et de continuer à itérer jusqu'à ce que le code soit sans bug et réponde à sa spécification. Cette idée de fermer la boucle a pris son essor vers la fin de l'année dernière, et elle a été un atout majeur pour permettre aux agents de codage de travailler plus longtemps de manière productive sans intervention humaine. Par exemple, ce week-end, je construisais une application pour ma fille afin qu'elle s'entraîne à taper, et mon agent de codage a pu facilement travailler pendant environ une heure, en utilisant un navigateur Web pour vérifier plusieurs fois ce qu'il avait construit avant de me le rendre, sans avoir besoin de mon intervention. La boucle d'ingénierie s'exécute rapidement. Toutes les quelques minutes, l'agent de codage peut construire et tester une nouvelle version du logiciel. J'entends fréquemment parler de développeurs qui trouvent de nouvelles façons d'ingénierer des boucles d'ingénierie plus efficaces. C'est un domaine d'invention actif ! Boucle de feedback développeur : Dans cette boucle, un développeur examine le produit actuel et dirige l'agent de codage pour l'améliorer. L'année dernière, beaucoup de développeurs (y compris moi) agissaient comme fonction QA (assurance qualité) pour nos agents de codage, trouvant manuellement des bugs et demandant ensuite à l'agent de les corriger. Mais avec les agents de codage capables de tester leur propre code beaucoup mieux, la quantité de temps que nous devons consacrer à cette fonction a considérablement diminué. Cela nous permet de prendre des décisions de produit de plus haut niveau, telles que les fonctionnalités clés à offrir, où l'interface utilisateur nécessite une amélioration, et ainsi de suite. La boucle de feedback développeur fonctionne sur des intervalles de temps entre dix minutes et plusieurs heures - c'est la fréquence à laquelle un développeur peut examiner un produit et donner son avis. Dans le cas de l'application de frappe, j'ai changé d'avis plusieurs fois sur la conception visuelle, les costumes de chat qu'elle peut débloquer en apprenant (elle adore les chats), et le flux utilisateur pour qu'un adulte se connecte et dirige l'expérience d'apprentissage de l'enfant. Lorsqu'un développeur a une vision claire de ce qu'il veut construire, il faut encore beaucoup de travail pour traduire cette vision en une spécification qu'un agent de codage puisse implémenter. De plus, après que le développeur a vu une implémentation, il pourrait mettre à jour (ou peut-être clarifier) la spécification pour la diriger vers ce qu'il veut. Si vous constatez que le système rencontre à plusieurs reprises certains problèmes, la création d'un ensemble d'évaluations pour l'agent devient utile. Les équipes natives de l'IA utilisent de plus en plus l'IA pour aider à façonner la direction du produit, par exemple, en automatisant la collecte et l'analyse des données d'utilisation, en résumant les commentaires clients écrits et verbaux, ou en effectuant une analyse concurrentielle. Cependant, pour pratiquement tous les produits auxquels je suis associé, je considère que les humains ont un avantage contextuel significatif par rapport aux systèmes d'IA actuels - nous en savons beaucoup plus que le système d'IA sur les utilisateurs et le contexte dans lequel le produit doit fonctionner - et donc les humains jouent un rôle essentiel. Beaucoup de gens décrivent cette contribution humaine comme du "goût", mais je préfère y penser comme l'avantage contextuel des humains, car cela nous donne une voie plus claire pour aider les systèmes d'IA à s'améliorer. Cela souligne également pourquoi cette étape ne peut pas être automatisée : tant que l'humain sait quelque chose que l'IA ne sait pas, l'humain dans la boucle est nécessaire pour injecter cette connaissance dans le système. Boucle de feedback externe : Cela comprend un large éventail de tactiques comme demander à quelques amis leur avis, lancer auprès de testeurs alpha, ou mettre le code en production avec des tests A/B. Ces tactiques sont généralement lentes, prenant rarement moins de quelques heures et parfois des jours voire des semaines. Ces données éclairent la vision du développeur, qui à son tour continue de piloter la spécification détaillée du produit, qui à son tour pilote l'agent de codage. Avec les agents de codage qui accélèrent le développement logiciel, de plus en plus d'ingénieurs commencent à jouer un rôle partiel de gestion de produit. Pour de nombreux ingénieurs qui évoluent vers ce rôle, la partie la plus difficile est de façonner la vision du produit et de trouver un équilibre entre la construction (combler le fossé entre la vision et la spécification) et l'obtention des retours des utilisateurs pour faire évoluer la vision. Il est important de faire les deux ! J'écrirai davantage sur la façon de faire cela dans de futurs posts, mais pour l'instant, je trouve encourageant que les ingénieurs jouent un rôle élargi (tout comme les chefs de produit et les designers font maintenant plus d'ingénierie). tips.text_original: “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). [Original text: The Batch]

idees.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'appuyer en arrière, passer en mode vocal et juste "divaguer" pendant environ 10 minutes, le chaos total, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview de quelques échanges. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus clairement que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit-machine et avez moins à corriger par la suite.
idees.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

idees.text_fr: La modélisation du monde avec JEPA a récemment gagné du terrain grâce à un nouveau mécanisme anti-effondrement appelé "SIGReg" (par @ylecun et @randall_balestr ). Les maths sont élégantes, mais elles sont rarement expliquées à partir des principes fondamentaux, alors je les ai décortiquées dans un billet de blog détaillé 📰 Voici le résumé (🧵) : Le problème : dans JEPA, les deux côtés de la perte de prédiction passent par le même encodeur. Si chaque entrée est mappée à un point constant unique, le prédicteur le fait correspondre trivialement, et la perte atteint exactement zéro. Score parfait, information nulle. La descente de gradient trouve cette solution par défaut. Les travaux antérieurs ont contourné ce problème avec des stop-gradients, des modèles enseignant-élève EMA, des encodeurs pré-entraînés gelés et des pertes de type VICReg avec plus de 6 coefficients ajustés à la main. Chacun ajoute de l'instabilité, des hyperparamètres ou une dépendance à la pré-formation de quelqu'un d'autre. --- SIGReg remplace tout cela par un unique régularisateur basé sur une seule affirmation : forcer le lot d'embeddings à ressembler à des échantillons d'une gaussienne isotrope, N(0, I). LeJEPA prouve que ce n'est pas arbitraire. C'est la distribution qui minimise le risque en aval dans le pire des cas, à travers les sondes linéaires et non linéaires. Mais "rendre les embeddings gaussiens" est facile à dire et difficile à calculer. Vous ne pouvez pas estimer une densité dans plus de 200 dimensions à partir d'un petit lot. La solution est une chaîne de quatre résultats classiques : comparer les transformées de Fourier au lieu des densités, transformer cette comparaison en un seul scalaire, approximer l'intégrale avec environ 16 points, et élever le tout de 1D à n'importe quelle dimension avec un théorème de 1936. Chaque étape est simple. C'est l'ensemble qui le fait fonctionner. Lisez les publications suivantes de ce fil pour comprendre chaque étape. --- Mais pourquoi cela fonctionne de manière prouvable : la seule distribution pour laquelle SIGReg = 0 est N(0, I), qui est de rang complet par construction, avec chaque valeur propre égale à 1. Un encodeur effondré de rang faible ne peut pas être un minimum. Il n'est pas seulement peu probable qu'il y converge – c'est mathématiquement exclu. Et la boucle d'entraînement reste simple : `total loss = prediction + λ·SIGReg` L'encodeur reçoit des gradients des deux termes ; le prédicteur reçoit des gradients du terme de prédiction uniquement. Pas de mises à jour alternées, pas de stop-gradients, pas d'astuces à deux échelles de temps. Maintenant, consultez la décomposition ci-dessous. 👇
idees.text_original: World Modeling with JEPA has recently gained traction thanks to a novel anti-collapse mechanism called "SIGReg" (by @ylecun and @randall_balestr ). The math is clean, but it is rarely explained from first principles, so I broke it down in a detailed blog post 📰 Here is the summary (🧵): The problem: in JEPA, both sides of the prediction loss go through the same encoder. Map every input to a single constant point, the predictor matches it trivially, and the loss hits exactly zero. Perfect score, zero information. Gradient descent finds this solution by default. Prior work patched around it with stop-gradients, EMA teacher-student models, frozen pretrained encoders, and VICReg-style losses with 6+ hand-tuned coefficients. Each adds instability, hyperparameters, or a dependency on someone else's pretraining. --- SIGReg replaces all of that with one regularizer built on a single claim: force the batch of embeddings to look like samples from an isotropic Gaussian, N(0, I). LeJEPA proves this isn't arbitrary. It's the distribution that minimizes worst-case downstream risk across linear and nonlinear probes. But "make the embeddings Gaussian" is easy to say and hard to compute. You can't estimate a density in 200+ dimensions from a small batch. The fix is a chain of four classical results: compare Fourier transforms instead of densities, turn that comparison into a single scalar, approximate the integral with ~16 points, and lift the whole thing from 1D to any dimension with a theorem from 1936. Each step is simple. The stack is what makes it work. Read the subsequent posts in this thread to understand each step. --- But why it provably works: the only distribution for which SIGReg = 0 is N(0, I), which is full rank by construction, with every eigenvalue equal to 1. A collapsed low-rank encoder cannot be a minimum. It's not just unlikely to converge there—it's mathematically excluded. And the training loop stays boring: total loss = prediction + λ·SIGReg The encoder gets gradients from both terms; the predictor gets gradients from the prediction term only. No alternating updates, no stop-gradients, no two-timescale tricks. Now check out the breakdown below. 👇

SIGReg : un mécanisme technique pour stabiliser l'apprentissage des modèles JEPA. Embeddings : représentations numériques de données (comme du texte) dans un format que les IA peuvent comprendre. idees.text_fr: Adam Thierer a écrit le livre fondateur sur "l'innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas à demander la permission au gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. La protection de l'IA open source est maintenant un élément essentiel pour garantir cela. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) Nous sommes à un carrefour critique dans le débat sur la gouvernance de l'IA aux États-Unis, et il semble que nous nous rapprochions d'une bataille très sérieuse pour savoir si les modèles open source seront même autorisés dans un environnement où un nouveau régime de licence de facto a commencé à prendre forme. En l'absence de cadres statutaires formels du Congrès ou de règles claires de l'administration (comme la révision de la règle de diffusion), nous semblons être laissés avec un processus d'examen des modèles sporadique, arbitraire et non transparent. La fiction des accords "volontaires" plane sur ce débat, et certains grands développeurs de modèles montrent déjà une volonté incroyable de faire des courbettes pour satisfaire les officiels / ordres liés à la sécurité nationale dont le reste d'entre nous n'est pas au courant. C'est un processus très opaque. Et ces développeurs de modèles sont censés jouer le jeu avec ces officiels, sinon leurs modèles seront retirés du marché ou retardés pendant de longues périodes. Ou ils perdront tous les contrats d'approvisionnement gouvernementaux qu'ils ont. Il n'y a rien de "volontaire" à cela lorsque cette épée de Damoclès plane dans la pièce. Alors que ce désordre s'aggrave, à un moment donné, la question de savoir comment gérer les modèles open source prendra plus d'importance car elle le devra. J'ai même entendu quelques rumeurs récemment selon lesquelles quelque chose pourrait venir de l'administration à ce sujet. Il va sans dire que si ce nouveau régime informel d'examen des modèles d'IA s'étend et prend plus de caractéristiques / exigences de pré-vérification, il est difficile de voir comment les acteurs open source pourraient se conformer à une telle quasi-licence des modèles d'IA. Spécifiquement, si ce nouveau régime ambigu est accompagné d'une présomption générale de "restreindre jusqu'à autorisation", alors ce serait la fin pour l'open source. C'est un chemin très sombre pour notre pays. Pire encore, bien sûr, serait une mesure des responsables de la sécurité nationale pour restreindre plus directement les modèles et capacités open source. Si cela se produit, alors nous serions de retour au milieu d'une bataille similaire à celle de la "Clipper Chip" comme celle que nous avons vue à la fin des années 90. C'est un chemin beaucoup plus sombre pour l'Amérique. Pendant ce temps, les développeurs open source n'ont pas d' "actions d'or" ou d'autres avantages à offrir au gouvernement pour résoudre leurs problèmes. Soyons clairs : Si notre gouvernement prend le chemin sombre, ce sera la bataille la plus importante pour la liberté de calcul de l'époque moderne. Il est temps que les gens prennent position pour défendre l'open source avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m
idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m
